tier_reason: The only number is one first-party README sentence ('roughly 1.9x faster than samtools sort for template-coordinate order' on a 30M-read WGS BAM), repeated as '1.9x faster than samtools on template-coordinate sort' in fgumi's src/lib/commands/sort.rs help text; no benchmark code, hardware, thread count, memory limit or samtools version anywhere, so C.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 9 stars, 0 forks, 29 commits; published on crates.io as fg-mako and on Bioconda; sort engine comes from fulcrumgenomics/fgumi (57 stars)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Cargo [profile.release] lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, mimalloc allocator (Cargo.toml); rustc version, samtools version, build and command line not stated.
corrections.caveats: One first-party sentence with no hardware, thread count, memory limit, samtools version or command. The README defers 'detailed benchmarks' to the fgumi documentation, but fgumi's README, docs/src/guide/performance-tuning.md and best-practices.md (opened) carry no samtools timings; the only other occurrence is the bare '1.9x faster than samtools on template-coordinate sort' line in fgumi src/lib/commands/sort.rs. The two tools do not produce the same order: fgumi's best-practices.md says samtools sort --template-coordinate does not consult the tc tag when ordering secondary and supplementary reads and is not a substitute for fgumi sort, so the compared work differs. fgumi does BGZF (de)compression through libdeflate (C, via libdeflater) and uses mimalloc (C); whether the samtools build used libdeflate is unknown. mako is a thin packaging of fgumi's sort engine (all sort logic lives upstream); if fgumi is listed later, mako folds into it.
corrections.why_faster: Per the README and fgumi's sort.rs: parallel radix sort of in-memory chunks on raw BAM bytes, O(1) merge comparisons through pre-computed sort keys, spill-to-disk external merge; fgumi also uses libdeflate (C) for BGZF and mimalloc. No profile or ablation is published, so the share of each is unknown.

notes: Claim confirmed as a single unsupported first-party sentence; tier C stands. Shortcomings: no methodology at all (hardware, threads, memory, samtools version), compared outputs differ (samtools ignores the tc tag on secondary/supplementary reads), and mako is only a packaging of fulcrumgenomics/fgumi's engine (fgumi is not in the list; if it is added, record mako as duplicate). Metadata checked: MIT, last commit 2026-08-25, active.

tier_reason: First-party Criterion run with public code (benches/walk.rs), CPU model (Xeon E5-1630 v3) and minifind's profile flags in Cargo.toml, but rustc version and GNU find's version and build flags are not stated, so it falls short of A for the baseline side; C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --bench walk (Criterion 0.8, 80 s warm-up, 400 s measurement); the bench profile inherits Cargo.toml [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1; mimalloc allocator. rustc version not stated (rust-version floor 1.85.1); GNU find is whatever 'find' is on PATH, version and build flags not stated.
corrections.caveats: Win is mostly parallelism: minifind uses all 8 hardware threads (one reserved for output) while GNU find is single-threaded, and the README itself says the gap 'shrinks toward parity on a 1-2 core host'. Process startup is included for both; both tools' stdout is captured into a pipe by Command::output() and dropped. The benchmark does not check that the two outputs match; minifind defaults to one filesystem and types d/f/l, plain 'find' lists every type and crosses mounts (equivalent on a kernel clone). GNU find version and build flags (distribution packages are usually -O2) and rustc version are unstated. Numbers come from the 2026-06-19 'full-clock rerun' commit, made the same day the 'fd-anchored parallel walker' landed; warm page cache only, the README says the gap narrows on a cold cache. Single machine, one first-party run. Repo contains AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md (AI-assisted development).

notes: Numbers match the README exactly (26.634/26.702/26.779 ms vs 92.463/92.998/93.565 ms, about 3.5x). Shortcomings: parallel vs single-threaded baseline (not a codegen win; same_algorithm false), no output-equality check, GNU find build unstated. Related to sharkdp/fd (already listed, wave 14 C) but not a fork or port of it.

tier_reason: First-party hyperfine runs with public driver code (benches/bench_tools.rs), CPU (Apple M5 Max, 128 GB), tool versions (jq-1.8.1 via mise, rustc 1.93.1) and qj's release flags, but jq's build flags are not stated (mise installs the prebuilt release binary), so A fails on the baseline side; C.

corrections.baseline: jq 1.8.1 (C; prebuilt release binary installed by mise, build flags not stated); jaq 2.3.0 and gojq 0.12.18 also shown
corrections.claimed_speedup: benches/results_ndjson_medium.md (2026-09-30, Apple M5 Max 128 GB, hyperfine median of 3 runs, 1 warm-up, qj 0.1.4 vs jq-1.8.1), 3.4 GB GH Archive NDJSON: .actor.login 143.5 ms parallel / 1.32 s 1 thread vs jq 18.04 s (125.7x / 13.6x); select(.type == "PushEvent") 162.8 ms / 1.68 s vs jq 32.17 s (197.6x / 19.2x); {type,repo,actor} 152.1 ms / 1.46 s vs jq 19.83 s (130.4x / 13.6x). benches/results_json.md, 49 MB large_twitter.json, single file: 4.7x to 28.2x over jq (README rounds to 5-28x), e.g. '.statuses|map({user, text})' 35.5 ms vs 645.6 ms (18.2x); geometric mean 8.7x. Extended (514 MB): stdin 15.5-29.4x, slurp 5.2-5.7x. On a 4.7 GB file on an M4 Pro (1 run): 96.4-156.9x parallel, 4.5-28.6x single-thread.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: qj: Cargo [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = "thin", rustc 1.93.1 (mise.toml); vendored simdjson (C++) compiled by build.rs with opt_level(3). jq-1.8.1, jaq 2.3.0, gojq 0.12.18 and hyperfine 1.20.0 installed by mise (prebuilt binaries; jq's compiler flags not stated).
corrections.caveats: Most of the gain is not Rust codegen: single-file JSON is parse-bound (jq needs about 300 ms for '.statuses|length' alone, qj 24 ms; peak parse 1.2 GB/s vs jq 50 MB/s), and parsing is done by vendored C++ simdjson through FFI, with simple filters evaluated directly on simdjson's tape; the 125-198x NDJSON rows add mmap and parallel workers on every M5 Max P-core (parallel vs 1-thread is about 9-10x). VM-bound filters (group_by, sort_by, reduce) gain only about 5x, still mostly parse. qj uses 80-410 MB vs jq's ~6 MB on the 3.4 GB file. Numbers were measured on qj 0.1.4 (current 0.2.1). bench_tools.rs checks qj vs jq output only on the JSON files and benchmarks anyway when they mismatch. No top-level LICENSE file: MIT is declared in Cargo.toml, LICENSE-jq covers the ported jq core (MIT, with CC BY 3.0 docs and ICU-licensed parts), simdjson is vendored. Also a parked cross-wave lead (wave 4 json) in QUEUE.md. Young repo with a large commit count and a CLAUDE.md (AI-assisted development).
corrections.why_faster: SIMD parsing by vendored C++ simdjson (NEON/AVX2) via FFI, tape evaluation of simple filters without building jq values, mmap of file input, and parallel NDJSON workers (1 MB chunks, P-cores only on Apple Silicon); the rest is a Rust port of jq 1.8.1's VM. The parse-bound part of the win belongs to simdjson, a C++ library.

notes: Numbers verified in benches/results_ndjson_medium.md and results_json.md (README matches); the record's 'jq version not stated' was wrong (jq-1.8.1). Under the wave 14 wrapped-library rule, the win comes largely from vendored C++ simdjson (already listed, wave0-seed tier A) plus parallelism, so the orchestrator should consider decision duplicate of https://github.com/simdjson/simdjson for this domain, or keep it with that shortcoming (it is a genuine jq replacement that fits wave 4 json).
